Caregiver Resource

TEACH Toolkit

Teletherapy-Enabled Action for Caregivers at Home
Caregiver Resource Pediatric Occupational Therapy Teletherapy
Introduction

Welcome: What This Toolkit Is For

Teletherapy is different from going to a clinic. It happens at home, in real life. Your child may be tired, loud, silly, upset, distracted, or not ready to join. That is okay.

This toolkit is here to help you know what to do before, during, and after teletherapy sessions.

You are not expected to be the therapist. You do not have to make the session perfect. You do not have to make your child do everything right.

Your job is to stay nearby, help your child feel safe, and share what you notice with the therapist.

You already know your child best. You know their moods, their sounds, their hard moments, and what helps them calm down or try again.

This toolkit will give you simple ways to help with setup, materials, attention, behavior, and hard moments during teletherapy. These ideas use parenting skills you already have.

Even when a session feels messy, it can still help your child.

Getting Started

How to Use This Toolkit

Before your first session Read through the full toolkit once so you know what to expect. Section 1: Getting Ready for a Session is a good place to go deeper before you begin.
During a session Be present with your child and communicate what you notice to your therapist. Use the ideas in Section 2: What to Do During a Session as support when you need them.
When something isn't working Let the therapist know what you notice. Then follow the therapist's lead if the plan changes. You can come back to Section 3 later for more support.
After a session Write down one thing you noticed. That becomes your starting point next time. Before digging deeper, there is a Reflection and FAQ section at the end of the toolkit. Keep in mind what sections of the toolkit you would like to revisit before the next session.
01
Section 1

Getting Ready for a Session

A small amount of preparation can prevent common disruptions and help the session start smoothly. You do not need to get everything perfect. You just need to be ready enough, and this section shows you what that looks like.

What This Helps You Do

  • Set up your space so your therapist can see and guide effectively
  • Gather materials ahead of time so you are not scrambling mid-session
  • Reduce distractions so you can focus on your child
  • Start the session in a calm, ready state

Before Every Session: Quick Checklist

CategoryWhat to Have Ready
Technology Device charged or plugged in. Wifi connection checked. Camera and sound working. Do this five minutes before, not while the session is starting. Know how to reconnect if the call drops.
Space A spot where your child can move safely and still be seen on camera. Aim the camera so the therapist can see your child's face, hands, and work area. Try to use a space with good lighting and low background noise so everyone can see and hear clearly. Sit nearby, or stay close enough to step in quickly if your child needs help.
Materials Two or three of your child's favorite toys or familiar objects within reach. Any specific items your therapist asked you to have. Nothing elaborate. Familiar beats fancy every time.
Distractions Siblings occupied or in another room. TV off. Your phone on silent and face-down. You need to be able to focus on your child for the full session.
Your child It helps if your child is fed and well-rested, and we understand this can be hard to manage some days.
Yourself Take five minutes before the session to step away from what you were doing and use a calming strategy if needed so you can enter the session with a sense of calm rather than rushing. Your child often looks to you to understand how to respond. You are more prepared for this than you think.

How It Looks in Real Life

It is two minutes before the session starts. You plug in your device, set it where your child can be seen, and place two favorite toys nearby. You turn off the TV and silence your phone. Your child is moving around, and you sit close enough to step in when needed. Before logging on, you take one slow breath. When the therapist joins, you are ready to start instead of trying to set things up while the session is already happening.

What Other Parents Say

Once I started setting things up before the session, everything felt less chaotic and stressful. I wasn't scrambling anymore.

02
Section 2

What to Do During a Session

This section outlines the key actions you can use during a session to support your child's engagement and participation. You will use these the whole time, even when things are going well.

What This Helps You Do

  • Stay calm and steady during the session
  • Notice when your child's body, mood, or attention changes
  • Communicate clearly with your therapist
  • Support your child without taking over
  • Make small changes to keep the session moving
Core Tools

The 5 Actions: Quick Guide

Each builds on the one before it. Start with Action 1.

1 Calm Yourself First
Keeping yourself calm and steady.		 Your child often looks to you to understand how to react. When you are more settled, it helps them stay more settled too. Take one slow breath before the session starts · Use a quick reset if needed · Pause before reacting
2 Notice
Paying attention to what your child is doing.		 You can see things the therapist can't fully see on screen. What you notice helps guide the session. Watch your child more than the screen · Look for small changes
3 Narrate
Saying out loud what you are noticing.		 Your therapist depends on you to understand what is happening in the room. Say what you see in simple words · Add context if you have it · Let the therapist know what you're about to do
4 Join
Getting involved in the activity with your child.		 Children are more likely to try something when they see you doing it too. Sit close · Start the activity if they aren't engaging so they have a model to follow · Show interest · Step back once they get going
5 Be Open to Changes
Staying flexible when the plan changes.		 Not every activity will work every time. The therapist may change the plan to better fit what your child needs in the moment. Tell the therapist what you notice · Stay open if the plan changes · Follow the therapist's lead with the new approach
1
Action 1
Calm Yourself First

Teletherapy is different because the therapist is on a screen, and you are in the room with your child. If your child gets upset, runs away, avoids the activity, or has a hard time changing tasks, the therapist can guide you. But you are the person close enough to help in the moment.

This action is about calming your own body first. Your job is not to force your child to calm down, stop crying, or finish the activity right away. Your job is to stay as calm and steady as you can, so your child has calm to borrow from you.

This is called co-regulation. Co-regulation means your child uses your calm voice, face, and body to feel safer.

Hard moments are part of teletherapy. Your child may cry, refuse, run away, get silly, or stop listening. This does not mean the session is going badly. It means your child may be showing you that something feels too hard, too much, or unclear.

Your child is not trying to ruin the session. They are having a hard time. You do not have to take the behavior personally, and you do not have to fix it all at once.

When this happens, start with yourself. Take a breath. Drop your shoulders. Use fewer words. Then look to the therapist for help. The therapist can change the activity, but your calm body and steady voice can help your child feel safer while that happens.

Your job is not to make the session perfect. Your job is to calm yourself first, stay nearby, and tell the therapist what you notice.

How to Co-Regulate During Teletherapy

StepWhat to DoWhy It Helps
Calm your own body first Take one slow breath. Drop your shoulders. Use a quiet voice. Pause before you jump in. When you calm your own body, your child has calm to borrow.
Stay close, but do not take over Sit nearby, move closer, or get down on your child's level. Wait for the therapist's direction when you can. Your child may need you near them, but the therapist is still leading the session.
Use fewer words Say one simple thing at a time, like "I'm here," "Let's try," or "First this, then break." Too many words can make a hard moment harder. Simple words help your child know what to do next.
Show calm with your body Soften your face. Lower your voice. Sit beside your child. A calm body can help the room feel safer.
Make the task smaller Ask the therapist, "Can we make this easier?" or "Can we try just one step?" A smaller task can feel less scary or frustrating.
Try calming touch or movement if your child likes it Try a firm hug, rocking, swaying, pushing, pulling, or a short movement break, if your child likes these things. Some children feel safer with deep pressure or movement. The therapist can help you choose what fits your child.
Tell the therapist what you see Say things like, "She does better with less talking," or "He needs a minute before we try again." What you notice helps the therapist know what to try next.

See It in Action

During a teletherapy session, the therapist asks your child to switch from a favorite toy to an activity at the table. Your child starts to cry and moves away from the screen.

Instead of trying to make your child come back right away, you start with yourself. You pause, take a breath, lower your voice, and move closer. You remind yourself, "My child is having a hard time, not trying to give me a hard time."

Your child may still be upset, and that is okay. You stayed calm, gave your child support, and helped the therapist understand what was happening. The goal was not to force the activity. The goal was to help your child feel safe enough to try again.

Signs It's Clicking

  • You pause before jumping in during hard moments.
  • You use a calmer voice and fewer words when your child is upset.
  • You look to the therapist for help instead of trying to fix everything alone.
  • You can tell the therapist what helps your child calm down or try again.
  • Hard moments still happen, but you feel more ready to handle them.
2
Action 2
Notice

During teletherapy, your therapist can see what is on the screen, but you can see your whole child. You are in the room. You can see your child's body, face, hands, energy, and mood in a way the therapist may not be able to see clearly through the camera.

Your job is not to figure out what everything means. Your job is to notice what changes.

You know your child's patterns. You may notice when your child starts getting tired, silly, frustrated, quiet, wiggly, or ready for a break. These small changes matter during teletherapy because they help the therapist know when to adjust the session.

Your job is to notice changes in your child and share them with the therapist. The therapist's job is to use that information to adjust the session for your child.

Here's What to Know

Try to watch your child more than the screen. You can still look at the therapist when needed, but your best information comes from the child right in front of you.

Noticing can be simple. Look for changes in:

AreaWhat You Might Notice
BodyMoving away, leaning on you, falling to the floor, wiggling more, getting still
FaceLooking worried, blank, excited, frustrated, tired, or close to tears
VoiceGetting louder, quieter, silly, upset, or not answering
HandsFidgeting more, throwing, grabbing, refusing, or stopping
AttentionLooking away, leaving the activity, watching without joining, or needing more help
EnergySpeeding up, slowing down, getting wild, shutting down, or needing movement

You do not need to know exactly why it is happening. The helpful part is noticing that something changed.

What to Say

Keep it short. You can simply name what you see.

"She is getting louder." "He moved away." "She stopped answering." "He is looking at me now." "She seems tired." "He is still listening, but he is not looking." "This is usually when things get hard for us."

After you share what you notice, the therapist can decide what to do next.

See It in Action

Your child has been part of the session for ten minutes. Then they start getting louder and sillier. You know this often happens before things get harder.

You do not need to figure out why it is happening. You do not need to fix it.

You simply say, "He is getting louder and sillier. This is usually when things start to get hard."

The therapist uses that information to adjust the session. They might make the activity shorter, add movement, give fewer directions, or offer a break.

You noticed the change. That was enough.

Signs It's Clicking

  • You watch your child more than the screen.
  • You notice small changes before things get harder.
  • You name what you see without feeling like you have to explain it.
  • The therapist uses what you notice to guide the session.
  • You feel less pressure to fix everything yourself.
3
Action 3
Narrate

Once you notice something, say it out loud. A lot happens in the room that the therapist may not see on the screen. When you name what you see, you give the therapist helpful information right away.

You do not need to explain it perfectly. You do not need to know why it is happening. Use short, simple words. The therapist will use what you share to decide what to do next.

Here's What to Know

Narrating means saying what you see in the moment. Keep it simple and factual, like you would in a quick text. You might say:

"She is getting louder." "He moved away." "She went quiet." "He is looking at the door." "He tried it once and stopped." "She does better with fewer words."

One short sentence can help.

See It in Action

The therapist is leading an activity. Your child tries it once, then turns away and starts looking at the door. You say: "He's looking at the door. I think he hears the dog." The therapist pauses and gives your child a moment. The activity picks back up thirty seconds later.

Signs It's Clicking

  • The therapist is responding to what you say and using it to adjust.
  • You are saying things out loud that you used to keep to yourself.
  • The session feels like a team effort, not something you are just watching.
  • You made it a team effort. That is not a small thing.
4
Action 4
Join

During teletherapy, the therapist may ask your child to try something through the screen. This can be hard for young children. They may not know what to do first, where to look, or how to get started.

This is where you can help.

Joining means you take part just enough to help your child begin. You are not doing the activity for your child. You are showing them, "This is safe. This is something we can try."

You already do this in everyday life. You help your child try new things by sitting near them, showing interest, and taking the first small step. Teletherapy uses those same strengths.

Here's What to Know

When your child is unsure, your joining can make the activity feel easier. You can pick up the toy, touch the material, start the movement, or do one small part of the activity. Then pause and give your child space to try.

You do not need to make the activity exciting. You do not need to perform for the camera. You do not need to get your child to do it perfectly. Your job is to help your child see the first step and feel safe enough to join in. The therapist is still leading the session. You are helping your child connect to what the therapist is asking.

How to Join

1
Sit near your child

Sit close enough to help, but give your child room to try. Side by side often works well. This lets your child see you and the activity without feeling crowded.

2
Pick up or touch the activity materials

If your child is not engaging, start the activity yourself. Stack the blocks. Pick up the crayon. Start drawing.

"Look, I'm going to try this."   Or: "Let's see what happens if we do it this way."
3
Show interest

Comment on what you are doing. Be curious out loud. Your child watches your face to decide if something is worth their attention.

"Oh, this is interesting."   Or: "I wonder what this does."   Or: "Hm, this part is tricky."
4
Step back when your child joins in

Once your child is engaged, reduce your involvement gradually. The goal is to get them going, not to do it for them. If they disengage again, step back in. This is a rhythm, not a one-time action.

See It in Action

The therapist introduces a stacking activity. Your child glances at it and looks away. You pick up a block and start stacking, saying "I wonder how tall I can get this." Your child watches. After a few seconds, they reach for a block. You step back and let them take over.

Signs It's Clicking

  • Your child is engaging in the activity, even if they started by watching you.
  • You are stepping in and stepping back naturally, following their lead.
  • The therapist can keep the session going because your child is in it.
  • Your child joined with your support. You helped them find a way into the activity.
5
Action 5
Be Open to Changes

After you join the activity, your child may begin to participate. They may watch, copy, reach, move closer, or try one small part.

Sometimes, even after you join, the activity still does not work. Your child may turn away, get upset, stop trying, get silly, or seem stuck.

That is okay. Teletherapy does not always follow the plan exactly.

Your therapist may need to change the activity, make it smaller, give your child more time, add movement, or try a different way. Your role is not to decide the change on your own. Your role is to stay open, stay nearby, and help your child follow the new plan.

Here's What to Know

A changed activity is not a failed activity. It means the therapist is using what is happening in the moment.

If your child is having a hard time, you can tell the therapist what you see. Then wait for the therapist to guide the next step.

Then the therapist may change the activity. They may ask you to use fewer materials, try one step, give your child a break, move to the floor, or use something your child already likes.

Your job is to be ready to shift with them.

When the Plan Changes

When You See ThisWhat Your Therapist Might Try
Child is completely stuck Break the task into a smaller step or simplify the activity
Child is trying but frustrated Slow the task down, give more time, or change how it is presented
Child is getting loud, overwhelmed, or reactive Pause the activity and shift to helping your child settle before continuing
Activity is not working at all Change the activity or try a different approach
Child has moved away but is still nearby Lower the demands and allow space for your child to re-engage

See It in Action

The therapist introduces a block activity. You join by sitting nearby and placing one block on the table. Your child watches for a moment, picks up a block, then turns away and pushes the materials back.

Instead of trying to make your child finish the activity, you stay calm and say, "He tried it once, but now he is turning away."

The therapist changes the plan. She asks you to use only two blocks and try one small step. You stay nearby, follow her lead, and help your child try the smaller version.

The activity changed, but the session kept going. You did not have to fix it. You stayed flexible and helped your child move with the new plan.

Signs It's Clicking

  • You understand that the plan may change during teletherapy.
  • You tell the therapist what you notice without feeling like you have to solve it.
  • You stay calm when the therapist changes the activity.
  • You help your child follow the new plan in a smaller or different way.
  • You feel less pressure to make the first activity work perfectly.
03
Section 3

When Things Don't Go as Planned

This section provides strategies to use when sessions become difficult, including how to respond to common challenges.

Before using any of the responses below:

Use Action 1 first. When you are overwhelmed, it is harder to use these tools. That is just how it goes.

What This Helps You Do

  • Respond when your child refuses or disengages
  • Stay present during difficult moments
  • Know what to try when something is not working
  • Learn from hard moments so the next session can work better
Core Tools

Before You Try Anything

Start with yourself first. Take one slow breath or use a quick calming strategy. The core actions from Section 2 still apply here. This section shows you how to use them when things are harder.

If/Then Guide

Your child refuses to start the session Do not force it. Let the therapist know. Start with something your child is already doing. Use joining (Action 4) to ease in through their current activity rather than the planned one.
Your child wanders away from the screen Follow them. Stay present. Keep low-level engagement going. Tell the therapist: "She's moved away. I'm going to stay with her." Do not try to drag them back.
Your child has a meltdown Stop the activity. Tell the therapist: "We need a minute." Focus on calming your own body first and helping your child feel safe. Do not worry about getting back to the activity right away.
The activity is not working anymore Tell the therapist what you see and ask what they want to try next. A session that changes direction is still a useful session.
You feel overwhelmed Start with yourself first. Take one slow breath, drop your shoulders, and use a quiet voice. You do not have to fix everything right away. If you need a pause, tell the therapist, "I need a minute." Then stay nearby and let the therapist guide the next step.
Technology fails Keep interacting with your child while you reconnect. The session does not stop because the screen freezes. Text or call your therapist to let them know you are reconnecting.
You are not sure if you are doing it right If you are present, watching your child, and trying to follow the therapist's lead, you are doing the main things this toolkit asks of you. Ask the therapist at the end of the session: "Is there anything I should do differently?" They will tell you.
Nothing seemed to work in the whole session Pick one thing you noticed and share it with the therapist. You might say, "He needed more time," "The noise was too much," "She stayed closer when I sat nearby," or "He did better when we stopped talking for a minute." The session still gave helpful information, even if it felt hard. That one detail can help the next session go better.

Every family has them. The ones who make progress are not the ones whose sessions always go well. They are the ones who show up again the next week.

How It Looks in Real Life

Your child refuses to join and walks away. You feel the urge to bring them back right away.

Instead, you pause and take a breath. You follow your child and stay nearby. You say, "She's not ready right now. I'm going to stay with her."

The therapist changes the plan while you keep a small connection with your child. You might sit nearby, hold the toy, talk softly, or simply stay close without pushing.

After a few minutes, your child starts to come back.

The session did not go as planned, but it still helped. You and the therapist learned that your child may need more time, less pressure, or a different way to start.

What Other Parents Say

Some sessions felt like a total mess, but those were actually the ones where we figured out what my child needed.

✓
You Are Ready

Reflection and FAQs

This section helps you make sense of what happened during a session and decide what to carry forward. Every time you show up, something useful happens. Even the sessions that feel like a complete disaster. Noticing what your child needs and trying to respond to it, even when it does not go perfectly — that is exactly what this is supposed to look like.

What This Helps You Do

  • Notice what worked during the session
  • Recognize small signs of progress
  • Decide what to try next time
  • Share useful information with your therapist

After Each Session: Reflect for Two Minutes

Optional but useful. The more you notice, the more you bring to the next session. You noticed more than you think. These questions help you find it.

One thing I noticed about my child today:
One thing that worked, even a little:
One thing to try differently next time:

Small Signs of Progress

Progress can be hard to see at first. It often shows up in small ways.

  • Your child stays engaged a little longer than last time
  • Your child comes back after walking away
  • Your child needs a little less help to settle
  • The session recovers after a hard moment

These are real changes, and they happened because you kept showing up. Write one down after the session if you can. Small changes add up over time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Questions Parents Ask

How much should I talk during a session?
Use short, simple comments when something changes. You do not need to talk the whole time. Say what you notice, then let the therapist guide the next step.
What if I disagree with something the therapist suggests?
Say so. You know your child and your home. If a suggestion does not fit, telling the therapist is more useful than trying to make it work.
My child ignores the video call entirely. Is this even working?
Probably yes. Children often take in more than it looks like. Listening without looking still counts. If your child stays in the room and occasionally engages, that counts. Talk to your therapist about what you are seeing.
How do I know if I am stepping in too much?
A simple rule: if your child is trying, step back. If your child is stuck or becoming upset, step in. Your therapist can also tell you when they want you to pull back. Ask them directly if you are not sure.
What if I miss a session or have to cancel?
Contact your therapist as soon as you know. Consistent attendance matters for progress but life happens. What matters most is coming back after a gap, not the gap itself.
Should I tell the therapist about things that happened between sessions?
Yes, always. Behaviors, reactions, small wins, hard moments: anything that seems related to what you are working on is useful. Start each session with one observation from the week.
What if my child does great in sessions but nothing changes at home?
That can happen, especially at first. Your child may need more time to use the skill in everyday life. Look for small times during the day when you can practice the same thing, like mealtime, getting dressed, bath time, or leaving the house. Tell the therapist what you are seeing at home so they can help you try it in a way that fits your child.
Am I supposed to do activities with my child between sessions?
Your therapist may suggest things to try during the week. These are not homework assignments. They are practice opportunities. Try them when they fit naturally into your routine. Report back what happened.

How It Looks in Real Life

The session felt messy. Your child walked away more than once. After it ends, you take a minute to think. You notice that your child came back on their own once and needed a little less help to settle. You write that down. At the next session, you share it with your therapist. That becomes the starting point for what to try next.

What Other Parents Say

At first it didn't feel like progress, but when I looked back, I could see small changes adding up.

You are not just watching the session. You are helping it work for your child.
